title.en: Language work for the poem on the magnifying glass: vocabulary, collective nouns, idioms with eye and the suffix -ish
Words that a magnifying glass reveals

text.en: A magnifying glass shows the tiny wonders of nature that our eyes miss: a spider, a hive of bees and even the moon within reach. The language work of this poem builds our vocabulary, collective nouns, idioms with the word eye and the suffix -ish, and helps us speak about space and inventions.

keepEnglishTerms: a swarm of locusts, a fleet of ships
apple of one's eye; in the blink of an eye
keep an eye on, turn a blind eye, see eye to eye, bird's-eye view

text.en:
Six useful words are woven, myriad, deft, stumble, surpass and marvellous. Woven means made by crossing threads, and here it means skilfully joined together. Myriad means countless, deft means quick and skilful, stumble upon means to find by chance, surpass means to go beyond, and marvellous means wonderful.
In the book's passage, a marvellous description, a story woven with fascinating details, a deft storytelling technique, myriad emotions, stumble upon twists and turns, and twists that surpass our understanding complete the paragraph.
A collective noun names a group. The poem uses 'a hive of bees'. In the same way we say a swarm of locusts, a constellation of stars, a grove of trees, a troupe of dancers, a battalion of soldiers and a fleet of ships.
An idiom has a meaning different from its separate words. The apple of one's eye is a person who is very precious. In the blink of an eye means something that happens very quickly.
To keep an eye on someone means to watch closely. To turn a blind eye is to act as if you do not see or notice. To see eye to eye is to agree with each other, and a bird's-eye view is an overall look at something, as if from above.
The poet uses the adjective 'tigerish' by adding the suffix -ish to the noun tiger. In the same way girl gives girlish, boy gives boyish and book gives bookish. The suffix -ish means like or somewhat like the noun.
Not every noun takes -ish; for glass we make glassy and for silk we make silken or silky. When unsure, check a dictionary.
For the listening task you hear a father and daughter talk about lesser-known Indian inventions. Read all six statements first, then mark the four that are true, listening for the attitude of the speakers, such as pride, excitement and surprise.
For the speaking task, learn the difference between the sounds f and v. For both, the lower lip lightly touches the upper teeth. The v sound has a vibration, but the f sound does not.
Practise f in forest, flowers, from, deft, afternoon, of and itself, and v in vase, valour, victory, woven, even, marvellous and hive.
Another speaking task asks which planet you would visit and why, with five things you would take. A third asks about a wonder invention you would make: say what it is, how it works and why it is needed, giving reasons.

problem.en: Match 'a fleet of' with the right word and say what 'turn a blind eye' means.

why.en: A fleet is a group of ships.

text.en: To turn a blind eye is to act as if you do not see or notice something.

why.en: It is an idiom, so it cannot be explained word by word.

prompt.en: Explain what a collective noun is and give two examples.

requiredIdeas.en: a collective noun names a group of people, animals or things
a correct example such as a swarm of locusts
a second correct example such as a grove of trees

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking a collective noun names only one person
Using the wrong group word, such as a fleet of locusts

points.en: Woven, myriad, deft, stumble, surpass and marvellous are useful words from the lesson.
Collective nouns: swarm of locusts, constellation of stars, grove of trees, troupe of dancers, battalion of soldiers, fleet of ships.
Eye idioms: apple of one's eye, in the blink of an eye, keep an eye on, turn a blind eye, see eye to eye, bird's-eye view.
The suffix -ish makes adjectives: girlish, boyish, bookish.
The v sound vibrates, the f sound does not.
